title: Running MongoDB: replica sets, sharding and the balancer
goal: By the end you can set up a MongoDB replica set and say what each member setting does, read its oplog window, explain how mongos, the config servers and the balancer place and move a sharded payments collection, and choose a shard key that neither piles every insert onto one shard nor makes the busiest read ask every shard.

warmup.q: A payments collection is sharded over three shards on `{ createdAt: 1 }`, and the balancer has evened out the data: each shard holds about a third. At 09:00 card traffic starts, 3,000 inserts a second. How are those inserts spread?
options: About 1,000 a second on each shard, because the data is balanced
All 3,000 on one shard, the one that owns the chunk ending at MaxKey
mongos sends them round-robin, and the balancer moves them into place later
Evenly, because MongoDB hashes every shard key before it cuts chunks
warmup.why: Balance describes data already stored. Each chunk owns a range of `createdAt`, and every new payment is later than all the others, so every insert falls in the last range, the one that ends at MaxKey, and one shard owns it. The balancer can move old ranges away afterwards, but at 09:00 one primary takes all 3,000 writes. MongoDB hashes a key only when you shard with `"hashed"`.

sections.h: One member: mongod, WiredTiger and the oplog
sections.body:
Lesson 8 of this track, Document stores with MongoDB, ran a replica set and broke it. This lesson and the next go inside two stores and set them up: MongoDB here, DynamoDB next. Start with one machine.

A MongoDB server is one process, `mongod`. It listens on port 27017 and keeps its data in files under `--dbpath` (`/data/db` in the lab containers). The code that lays documents out on disk is the storage engine, WiredTiger. It keeps each collection and each index as a B-tree (a sorted tree of pages; lesson 4 of the database internals track, B+trees, builds one) in a file of its own, compressed with snappy. The pages you use stay in WiredTiger's cache, by default the larger of 50% of (RAM minus 1 GB) and 256 MB, so a 16 GB server gives it 7.5 GB. Every 60 seconds WiredTiger writes a checkpoint, a consistent snapshot of every file. Between checkpoints its journal, a write-ahead log that each change is appended to first, records every change, so a crash loses nothing the journal has. The lab containers shrink the cache to 0.25 GB with `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB`.

One machine has lesson 8's problem: when it dies, payments stop. So you keep copies, and copies need a way to stay the same. Copying data files doesn't work, because they change while you copy. MongoDB copies operations instead. Every write the primary applies is also recorded in the oplog, the collection `local.oplog.rs`. It's a capped collection: fixed in size, kept in insertion order, oldest entries dropped when it's full. Each entry describes one change, usually to one document. Secondaries pull new entries and apply them in the same order.

One rule makes the copying safe: every oplog entry is idempotent, so applying it twice gives the same result as applying it once. The primary therefore doesn't log what you asked for, `$inc: { amountMinor: 100 }`, but what came out of it, `amountMinor: 4350`. A secondary that crashes halfway through a batch applies the whole batch again, and ends in the same state. The Try-it shows the rewrite.

The oplog's size decides how long a member may be away. By default it's 5% of the free disk, at least 990 MB and at most 50 GB. The time between its oldest and newest entry is the oplog window. A secondary that returns within the window replays what it missed. One that was away longer has lost entries it needed and must copy every document again, an initial sync, which for 2 TB of payments can take most of a day. Do the sum for your write rate: at 2 GB of oplog an hour, a 50 GB oplog holds 25 hours. If a member can be down for a long weekend, raise the size with `replSetResizeOplog` or set a floor in hours with `oplogMinRetentionHours`.

**Every MongoDB deployment is built from one part, the replica set: a primary orders writes in its oplog and secondaries replay it. A sharded cluster is several replica sets, each holding a slice of the data, plus one more replica set that holds the map of which slice lives where.** The rest of the lesson builds that picture, one box at a time.

sections.h: Set up a replica set: members, priorities and elections
sections.body:
A replica set is set up in two steps. Start every member with the same set name, then tell one of them who the members are:

```javascript
// each member was started with: mongod --replSet rs0 --bind_ip_all
rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [
  { _id: 0, host: "mongo1:27017", priority: 2 },
  { _id: 1, host: "mongo2:27017" },
  { _id: 2, host: "mongo3:27017" } ] })
```

`env/mongo-rs.yml` runs exactly this from mongo1's healthcheck. mongo1 stores the configuration, the others fetch it, and within seconds they elect a primary.

The election protocol, protocol version 1, derives from Raft, which lesson 12 of the database internals track, Replication and consensus with Raft, builds: members elect a leader by majority vote, and each election has a number, the term, so nobody votes twice in one term. Members send each other a heartbeat, a small "I'm alive" message, every 2 seconds. A secondary that hears nothing from the primary for `electionTimeoutMillis`, 10 seconds by default, becomes a candidate. It adds one to the term, votes for itself and asks the others. A member gives one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own. Votes from a majority of the voting members, 2 of 3, make a primary. The docs say the median election finishes within 12 seconds. A member with a higher priority calls elections sooner and, once it has caught up, takes the primary role back. Priority 0 means it never becomes primary.

Three member settings exist for special jobs:

- `hidden: true` (with priority 0): drivers never send it reads. Use it for backups or a nightly report.
- `secondaryDelaySecs: 3600` (with hidden, priority 0 and `votes: 0`): applies the oplog an hour late. If a bad deploy runs `deleteMany({})` on payments, this member still has them for an hour. The delay must be shorter than the oplog window.
- `arbiterOnly: true`: votes, holds no data. Avoid it. With a primary, a secondary and an arbiter, losing the secondary leaves one copy, and `w: "majority"` writes (lesson 8: acknowledged once a majority of members have them) stall, because the only other voter can't store them. A third data-bearing member costs one more disk and is a real copy. Since 5.3 MongoDB refuses a second arbiter unless you set `allowMultipleArbiters`.

A set can have up to 50 members, at most 7 of them voting.

Reads have a setting too. Read preference picks the member that serves a read. The default, `primary`, sees every acknowledged write. `secondary`, `secondaryPreferred` and `nearest` spread reads out, but a secondary is behind by its replication lag: milliseconds normally, minutes during a long index build or a network problem. `maxStalenessSeconds` (90 at least) tells the driver to skip a secondary that has fallen further behind. Read a balance before a payment from the primary. A month-end statement can come from a secondary.

try.title: Step the primary down and watch the term
steps: With `env/mongo-rs.yml` still up, run the commands below from the `labs` folder, in order. `rs.stepDown(20, 5)` asks mongo1 to step down and not stand again for 20 seconds, after waiting up to 5 seconds for a secondary to catch up.
Predict the term after the step-down, which member becomes primary, and what happens once the 20 seconds are over (mongo1 has priority 2).
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
# the members and the election settings
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'rs.conf().members.map(m => m.host + "  priority " + m.priority + "  votes " + m.votes)'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'const c = rs.conf().settings; ({ electionTimeoutMillis: c.electionTimeoutMillis, heartbeatIntervalMillis: c.heartbeatIntervalMillis, term: rs.status().term })'

# step down for 20 seconds, then look from mongo2
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'rs.stepDown(20, 5).ok'
sleep 5
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo2 mongosh --quiet --eval 'const s = rs.status(); ({ term: s.term, members: s.members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr) })'

# after the 20 seconds
sleep 30
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'const s = rs.status(); ({ term: s.term, members: s.members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr), why: s.electionCandidateMetrics.lastElectionReason })'

sections.h: Past one replica set: shards, config servers and mongos
sections.body:
A replica set puts every document on every member, and that gives it two ceilings. The data must fit one machine's disk, and the part you read must fit its cache: with 3 TB of payments and a 7.5 GB cache, most reads go to disk. And every write goes through one primary. If it takes 8,000 inserts a second at 70% CPU and Black Friday needs 25,000, more secondaries don't help, since each one replays all 25,000 writes too.

So split the collection over several replica sets. Build it up.

Version 1 splits in the application: accounts A-0000 to A-4999 on set 1, the rest on set 2, a rule in every service. It works until set 1 fills up. A third set means a new rule in every service at the same moment, and moving data while payments keep arriving.

Version 2 turns the rule into data: a table of key ranges and the set that holds each one. That table is now the most important data in the cluster, so it lives in a replica set of its own. And services shouldn't each read it: they talk to a router that reads it, keeps a copy in memory and forwards each operation. That's MongoDB's sharded cluster, in the figure:

- A shard is a replica set (three members in production) holding part of each sharded collection.
- The config server replica set holds the cluster's metadata in the `config` database: `config.shards`, `config.collections`, and `config.chunks`, which lists every range and its shard. It allows no arbiters and no delayed members. The balancer runs on its primary. If it can't elect a primary, the map is read-only: reads and writes go on, but nothing moves.
- `mongos` is the router. It has no data and nothing on disk. Applications connect only to mongos, so run several, often one next to each application instance.

A sharded collection has a shard key, a field or fields in its documents, and its key space is cut into chunks (the 9.0 docs also call them ranges), each owned by one shard. For an insert, mongos computes the document's shard key, finds the chunk whose range holds it and sends the insert to that shard's primary. A query whose filter pins down the shard key is targeted: mongos asks only the shards that own matching chunks, and `explain()` says `SINGLE_SHARD` when that's one. A query without the shard key goes to every shard and mongos merges the answers, a scatter-gather read, `SHARD_MERGE` in `explain()`. It's as slow as the slowest shard and every shard pays for it, so more shards don't make it faster.

To build one: start shard members with `mongod --shardsvr --replSet shard1`, config members with `mongod --configsvr --replSet cfg`, initiate each set as in the previous section, start `mongos --configdb cfg/cfg1:27017`, and on mongos run `sh.addShard("shard1/shard1:27017")` for each shard. `env/mongo-sharded.yml` does all of that, with one member per set to fit your laptop. Since 6.0 you don't need `sh.enableSharding()` first: `sh.shardCollection()` creates what's missing.

sections.h: The shard key decides where inserts land and which reads scatter
sections.body:
mongos can only route by the shard key, so the key decides two things: which shard each insert goes to, and which reads are targeted. Judge a candidate by three properties first.

Cardinality is the number of distinct values. All documents with one value live in one chunk, so a key with 3 values can never use more than 3 shards. `currency` on EUR, USD and GBP payments is that key.

Frequency is how often the commonest value appears. Shard on `merchantId`, and M-0042, with a fifth of all payments, sits in one chunk that grows without limit. A chunk bigger than the chunk size that can't be split, because every document in it has the same shard key value, is a jumbo chunk. The lab makes one.

A monotonic key only grows: `createdAt`, a sequence number, or the `ObjectId` that MongoDB puts in `_id` when you don't, whose first 4 bytes are a timestamp. The last chunk's range ends at MaxKey, a special value above every other, and every new value is beyond all the existing ones, so every insert goes to that last chunk on one shard. The Try-it puts 20,000 ledger entries on shard1 and none on shard2.

Then choose how the key is cut. Ranged sharding cuts the values in their order: neighbours stay together, so a range of the key is targeted. Hashed sharding, `{ _id: "hashed" }`, cuts the hash of the value instead. A growing key's inserts spread evenly, and an equality on the key is targeted, but a range is scattered, because neighbours hash far apart. A compound key with a hashed prefix mixes the two. Under `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }` accounts spread evenly over the shards, and one account's payments sit together in time order, the way lesson 3, Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics, built items with `ACCT#` and a time in the sort key.

Now test the candidates against the payments access patterns from lesson 2, Model the access patterns first:

| Shard key | Inserts | Account's newest payments | Payment by id | Merchant dashboard |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `{ createdAt: 1 }` | all on one shard | scatter | scatter | scatter |
| `{ merchantId: 1 }` | M-0042's shard is hot; jumbo chunk | scatter | scatter | targeted |
| `{ _id: "hashed" }` | even | scatter | targeted | scatter |
| `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }` | even | targeted | scatter | scatter |

For the payments core, take the last one. The account screen is the busiest read, and there are millions of accounts, each with a few payments a day. Give the merchant dashboard its own path, such as a reporting copy fed by a change stream (MongoDB's feed of committed changes, read from the oplog). Write the payment id lookup with the account id in the filter where you can.

One more rule follows from the key: MongoDB enforces a unique index across the cluster only if the shard key is its prefix. Even `_id` is unique only per shard when it isn't the shard key. So the idempotency key from lesson 8 can't have a unique index on a collection sharded by account. Keep claims in a collection of their own, with the idempotency key as `_id` and as the shard key, as lesson 3 did in DynamoDB.

A ranged key on an empty collection starts as one chunk, `[MinKey, MaxKey)`, on the database's primary shard, and no insert splits it, so all 20,000 entries are on shard1 and shard2 owns nothing. The balancer calls that compliant: about 19 MB is far below three times the default chunk size, 384 MB. A query on the newest entries is targeted, which sounds good, but it's targeted at the same shard that takes every write. stepper.title: The balancer moves a range off the hot shard
stepper.intro: The ledger from the Try-its, chunk size 1 MB: one migration, a stale router, and the hot last chunk.

frames.say: Every ledger entry is later than the one before, and one chunk covers the whole key space, `[MinKey, MaxKey)`, on shard1. mongos looks up the last entry's `createdAt`, 05:33:19, in its cached copy of the map and sends the insert to shard1's primary, which writes it and its oplog entry. No split happens on insert: since MongoDB 6.0.3 inserts never split a chunk.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 300" role="img" aria-label="The balancer sees 20 MB against 0 MB and cuts the range MinKey to 00:17:33 off the big chunk"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box-b" x="16" y="16" width="318" height="112" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="30" y="38" text-anchor="start">config primary: balancer round</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="30" y="62" text-anchor="start">shard1 20 MB, shard2 0 MB</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="30" y="82" text-anchor="start">difference >= 3 x 1 MB: move</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="30" y="102" text-anchor="start">cut [MinKey, 00:17:33)</text><rect class="box" x="350" y="16" width="314" height="112" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="364" y="38" text-anchor="start">mongos: cached copy</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="364" y="62" text-anchor="start">[MinKey, MaxKey)    shard1</text><rect class="box" x="16" y="152" width="318" height="136" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="30" y="174" text-anchor="start">shard1 primary</text><rect class="box-a" x="30" y="186" width="290" height="26" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="40" y="204" text-anchor="start">[MinKey, 00:17:33)  1,053 docs</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="218" width="290" height="26" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="40" y="236" text-anchor="start">[00:17:33, MaxKey)  18,947 docs</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="30" y="280" text-anchor="start">20 MB</text><rect class="box" x="350" y="152" width="314" height="136" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="364" y="174" text-anchor="start">shard2 primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="364" y="280" text-anchor="start">0 MB</text></svg>
frames.say: The balancer runs on the config server primary. It compares how many bytes of `sfz.ledger` each shard owns: 20 MB against 0. That's at least three chunk sizes (3 MB here, 384 MB at the default 128 MB), so it migrates. It cuts a range of about one chunk size off the big chunk, `[MinKey, 00:17:33)`, 1,053 entries, and that range is what moves.

frames.say: The balancer sends `moveRange` to shard1, the donor. shard2, the recipient, builds the collection's indexes, then pulls the range's documents. Nobody stops writing: during the copy, shard1 still owns the range and takes every write to it, and remembers those changes for later.

frames.say: shard2 applies the changes made during the copy until it's in step. shard1 holds writes to the range for a moment and commits the new owner in `config.chunks`. From now on shard2 owns the range. shard1's copies are orphans: still on disk, no longer owned, deleted later once no cursor reads them. mongos hasn't heard yet.

frames.say: A read for 00:05:00 arrives. mongos's copy still says shard1, so it asks shard1, which knows the range has a newer version and answers `StaleConfig`. mongos refreshes its routing table from the config servers and retries on shard2. Your service sees a slightly slower read, never an error.

try.title: Let the balancer move ranges, then add more entries
steps: In the same prompt, paste the block. It sets the ledger's chunk size to 1 MB, the smallest allowed, and waits 30 seconds. Predict how many ranges move, from which end of the time line, and where the next 1,000 entries go.
Type `exit`, then stop the cluster from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/mongo-sharded.yml down -v`.

code.title: in mongosh on mongos
code.src:
// pretend 1 MB is a full chunk: the balancer now acts at a 3 MB difference
db.adminCommand({ configureCollectionBalancing: "sfz.ledger", chunkSize: 1 }).ok
sleep(30000)
moves("ledger")      // the config servers' changelog: every committed migration
onShard("ledger")

// the next 1,000 entries: which shard takes them?
db.ledger.insertMany(ledger(1000, 20000)).acknowledged
onShard("ledger")
sh.status()          // look at the last chunks of sfz.ledger

Eight migrations in ten seconds, each a range of 17 minutes 33 seconds, 1,053 entries of about 1 KB: the balancer cut chunk-size ranges off the big chunk and moved them, starting at MinKey. It stopped at 11,576 against 8,424 owned, a difference just under 3 MB. shard1 still holds 8,424 orphans, the old copies of the moved ranges, which it deletes later. Then every one of the 1,000 new entries went to shard1, into the chunk that ends at MaxKey, because each was later than all the others. Run `moves("ledger")` again half a minute later and you'll see a ninth migration: the balancer chasing the shard that takes every write.

refs.title: MongoDB: the sharded cluster balancer (thresholds, migration steps)
MongoDB: data partitioning with chunks (range size, jumbo chunks)

analogy: Think of a payments archive that outgrew one building. It's split over several branch buildings, and each branch has a head clerk who files every new record in a day book and two assistants who copy it: a replica set. A central catalogue, kept in its own guarded office, lists which shelf ranges live in which branch: the config servers. Front desks in every office building look records up in a photocopy of the catalogue and send couriers to the right branch: mongos. At night a mover carts whole shelves from crowded branches to empty ones and updates the catalogue: the balancer. The analogy breaks in two places. MongoDB's mover works in daytime, while people keep adding records to the very shelf being moved, and that's why a migration copies first and catches up after. And a front desk's photocopy can be out of date, so a branch sometimes answers "not here any more" and the desk fetches a fresh copy, which is a StaleConfig error and a retry.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus payment service would connect to a list of mongos hosts, never to a shard, and the driver takes care of `StaleConfig` retries and of retryable writes after a failover. If you have used Oracle range partitioning by date, `{ createdAt: 1 }` will feel familiar, but on Oracle every partition lives in one database, so a hot newest partition costs you nothing extra. In a sharded cluster the newest range sits on one machine, and that machine takes every insert. The shard key works like the key of a Kafka record: it decides the partition, and one busy key (a merchant on Black Friday) overloads one partition whatever the cluster's size. Give idempotency claims their own collection with the key as `_id`, as you would with a unique constraint in Oracle, because a unique index on a sharded collection must start with the shard key.
mistake: The most common mistake is sharding on what the busiest query filters by, usually time: `{ createdAt: 1 }`, or the default `ObjectId` `_id`, which starts with a timestamp. It looks right in testing. Time-range queries are targeted, `sh.status()` shows balanced data, and the cluster runs fine at low traffic. In production every insert goes to the chunk that ends at MaxKey, one primary runs at 100% while the others idle, and the balancer spends its time moving yesterday's ranges off that shard. People make the choice because they read balance as the goal, when the goal is spread writes and targeted hot reads. The fix is a key whose leading part spreads writes, such as `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }`, checked against the real access patterns (and with `analyzeShardKey` on sampled queries) before the first shard is added. Changing the key later is a `reshardCollection`: a full copy of the collection.

worked.title: Set up a sharded payments cluster, from processes to a checked shard key

steps.say: Start the processes. Three members for the config servers, three for each shard, and one mongos per application host. Every member of a set gets the same `--replSet` name.
steps.code:
# config server replica set (on cfg1, cfg2, cfg3)
mongod --configsvr --replSet cfg --port 27019 --bind_ip_all --dbpath /data/cfg
# shard replica sets (on sh1a, sh1b, sh1c and sh2a, sh2b, sh2c)
mongod --shardsvr --replSet shard1 --port 27018 --bind_ip_all --dbpath /data/db
# routers, next to the payment service
mongos --configdb cfg/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27017 --bind_ip_all

steps.say: Initiate each replica set from one of its members. Same shape for every shard; `configsvr: true` marks the config servers.

On a mongos, add the shards, then shard payments on the key from the access patterns. On an empty collection MongoDB builds the shard key index itself and, for a hashed prefix, makes one chunk per shard.
Uniqueness that isn't the shard key gets a collection of its own. The idempotency key is the claim's `_id` and its shard key, so a duplicate fails on whichever shard owns it.
steps.code:
sh.shardCollection("sfz.idempotency", { _id: "hashed" })
db.idempotency.insertOne({ _id: "idem-7f3a", paymentId: "pay-81723", expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 86400000) })
db.idempotency.createIndex({ expiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 })   // a TTL index removes old claims

steps.say: Check the result before traffic arrives: the shards, the chunks, and that the account screen's query is targeted.
steps.code:
sh.status()
db.payments.getShardDistribution()
db.payments.find({ accountId: "A-1001" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan.stage
// SINGLE_SHARD: one account's payments live on one shard, in time order
// optional: keep migrations out of the peak
db.getSiblingDB("config").settings.updateOne({ _id: "balancer" },
  { $set: { activeWindow: { start: "23:00", stop: "05:00" } } }, { upsert: true })

lab.title: Build a shard-key simulator: chunks, routing and the balancer
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. All ten fail with `NotImplementedError`.
Read `ShardKeys.kt`. `Key` (with MinKey and MaxKey), `KeyRange`, `PaymentQuery` and `rangeFor` are given. Write `keyOf`: four one-line keys, one per pattern. The first test passes.

In `ShardedCluster.kt` the constructor already shards an empty collection the way MongoDB 8.0 and later do: one chunk per shard for a hashed prefix, one chunk on the first shard for a ranged key. Write `chunkFor` and `insert`. The `chunkFor` and hashed-spread tests pass: 30,000 payments land between 9,500 and 10,500 per shard.
Write `route`. The targeting test passes: the same merchant dashboard query is `SHARD_MERGE` under `{ _id: "hashed" }` and `SINGLE_SHARD` under `{ merchantId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }`.

Write `splitLargeChunks`, then `balancerRound`. The rest pass: 20 MB of time-ordered payments end at 8, 6 and 6 MB after 12 migrations, the next 1,000 inserts all hit the MaxKey chunk, and under `{ merchantId: "hashed" }` M-0042 becomes a 4 MB jumbo chunk that never moves.

Experiment: in `balancerRound`, change the threshold from 3 chunk sizes to 1 and run the balancing test again. It moves more chunks and ends closer to even. That's the trade the docs describe: small differences tolerated in exchange for fewer migrations.
hints: `chunks.floorEntry(key).value`: the chunks cover MinKey to MaxKey with no gaps, so there is always one. `Key` is `Comparable`, so `<=` and `>` work on keys.
A chunk `[min, max)` overlaps the inclusive range `[lo, hi]` when `min <= range.hi && max > range.lo`.
Runs: walk `chunk.keys.sorted()` and start a new run whenever the key differs from the current run's first key.

Packing: `if (current != null && (current.size + run.size).toLong() * docBytes <= chunkSizeBytes) current += run else pieces += ArrayList(run)`. Then remove the old chunk by its min and put each piece under its own min. Iterate over `chunks.values.toList()` so you don't change the map while walking it.

Pairing: sort once with `compareByDescending<String> { bytes.getValue(it) }.thenBy { shards.indexOf(it) }`, then walk inwards from both ends. `chunks.values.firstOrNull { it.shard == from && !it.jumbo }` is the donor's chunk with the smallest min, because a `TreeMap` iterates in key order.

drill.title: A replica set member list and a sharded collection, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the `rs.initiate` for a set `rs0` where mongo1 is preferred as primary and mongo3 is a hidden, one-hour delayed copy that doesn't vote. Then write the commands, run on mongos, that add one shard `shard1` (members sh1a, sh1b, sh1c on port 27018) and shard `sfz.payments` so that inserts spread and an account's newest payments are one targeted query. One line each: why no arbiter, and why not `{ createdAt: 1 }`.

recap: A `mongod` stores collections and indexes as WiredTiger B-trees, with a cache of the larger of 50% of (RAM minus 1 GB) and 256 MB, checkpoints every 60 seconds and a journal between them.

Replication copies operations: the primary writes idempotent entries (results, not `$inc`s) to the capped `local.oplog.rs`, and secondaries replay them. The oplog window is how long a member may be away without a full initial sync.

Elections follow a Raft-derived protocol: heartbeats every 2 s, a candidate after 10 s of silence, one vote per term, only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent. Priorities choose the preferred primary; hidden and delayed members do side jobs; arbiters are a false saving.

A sharded cluster is shards (replica sets), a config server replica set holding the chunk map and running the balancer, and stateless mongos routers. A filter with the shard key is targeted (`SINGLE_SHARD`); one without it scatters (`SHARD_MERGE`).

Pick a shard key with high cardinality, low frequency and no steady growth, that the busiest queries include. Monotonic keys put every insert on the MaxKey chunk; a dominant value makes a jumbo chunk; unique indexes must start with the shard key.

Since 6.0.3 inserts never split chunks. The balancer moves about one chunk size (128 MB default) at a time when shards differ by 3 chunk sizes, copying while writes continue. Fix a bad key with `refineCollectionShardKey` or a full `reshardCollection`.

quiz.q: A secondary of a 3-member set goes down for disk work on Friday evening and comes back on Monday morning, 60 hours later. `rs.printReplicationInfo()` on the primary says the log covers about 30 hours. What happens when the secondary restarts?
options: It replays the 60 hours from the primary's oplog and catches up
It finds that the oldest entry it needs was dropped, so it can't replay and needs an initial sync
The primary keeps oplog entries until every member has read them, so the oplog grew to cover the 60 hours
It becomes primary, because it has the oldest data
quiz.why: The oplog is a capped collection: when it's full, the oldest entries go, whether a member has read them or not. After 60 hours, the entries the secondary needs are gone, so it must copy every document again (an initial sync). The primary doesn't hold entries for absent members unless you set `oplogMinRetentionHours`, and even that is hours you choose in advance. Size the window for your longest planned absence.

quiz.q: Your team proposes primary, secondary and an arbiter to save one server. The secondary dies. What happens to `w: "majority"` payment writes?
options: They keep working: the arbiter's vote makes 2 of 3
They fail at once with an error saying the set has no majority
They can't be acknowledged: only one member can store data, and the arbiter can't store writes, so the writes wait until wtimeout
The arbiter stores the writes until the secondary returns
quiz.why: The arbiter votes, so the primary stays primary. But a write is acknowledged with `w: "majority"` only when a majority of members have it, and the arbiter holds no data, so the majority can't be reached and writes wait (until `wtimeout`, if you set one). The docs warn that majority writes in a primary-secondary-arbiter set have problems when the secondary is unavailable. A third data-bearing member keeps majority writes working through one failure.

quiz.q: A payments collection is sharded on `{ _id: "hashed" }`. Which of these queries does mongos send to a single shard?
options: `find({ accountId: "A-1001" })`
`find({}).sort({ _id: 1 }).limit(10)`
quiz.why: With a hashed key, mongos can target only an equality: it hashes `pay-81723` and asks the one shard whose chunk holds that hash. A range of `_id` values hashes to values all over the 64-bit space, so the range query goes to every shard, and so does the sort on `_id`. `accountId` isn't in the shard key at all, so that's a broadcast too. The Try-it showed `SINGLE_SHARD` for the equality and `SHARD_MERGE` without the key.

quiz.q: Under `{ merchantId: 1 }`, M-0042's chunk has grown to 9 GB while the chunk size is 128 MB. Why doesn't the balancer split it and spread it?
options: The balancer is switched off while a chunk is bigger than 1 GB
Every document in the chunk has the same shard key value, and a boundary can only fall between different values, so it's a jumbo chunk that can't be split or moved normally
Since 6.0.3 MongoDB never splits chunks at all
Chunks only split when you run `sh.splitAt()` by hand
quiz.why: All documents with one shard key value must live in one chunk, so a chunk of only M-0042's payments has nowhere to be cut: it's jumbo. The balancer doesn't move a chunk that's too big, and `moveRange` with `forceJumbo` blocks writes on the collection during the move. MongoDB still cuts ranges when it migrates; it only stopped splitting on insert in 6.0.3. The fix is a key with more values, such as `refineCollectionShardKey` to `{ merchantId: 1, createdAt: 1 }`.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: DynamoDB needed write sharding for a merchant taking 4,000 writes a second, because one partition key can't exceed 1,000 WCU. In a MongoDB cluster sharded on `{ merchantId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }`, does M-0042 still have a hot spot?
options: No: the hashed prefix spreads M-0042's payments over every shard
No: the balancer moves M-0042's newest range to a quiet shard every second
Yes: all of M-0042's new payments carry its one hash and the latest time, so they go to one chunk on one shard; the chunk can split by time, but the newest end is always in one place
Yes, but only on reads, because writes go to the primary of every shard
quiz.why: The hashed prefix spreads different merchants. Within one merchant the key is ordered by time, so M-0042's new inserts all land at its newest range, the same pattern as the hot last chunk, just per merchant. Adding `createdAt` cures the jumbo chunk (the range can now split), not the write hot spot. As in lesson 5, spreading one key's writes needs a suffix you choose, such as a shard number from `hash(paymentId) mod 10`, and reads that ask every suffix.

flashcards.front: Why does the oplog store `amountMinor: 4350` instead of `$inc: { amountMinor: 100 }`?
flashcards.back: Oplog entries must be idempotent: a secondary may apply an entry more than once (after a crash mid-batch) and must end in the same state.

flashcards.front: What is the default oplog size with WiredTiger?
flashcards.back: 5% of free disk space, at least 990 MB and at most 50 GB. Resize with `replSetResizeOplog`; set a floor in hours with `oplogMinRetentionHours`.

flashcards.front: When does a MongoDB secondary start an election, and who votes for it?
flashcards.back: After `electionTimeoutMillis` (10 s by default) without hearing the primary. It raises the term; each member votes once per term, only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own. A majority wins.

flashcards.front: What does each part of a sharded cluster hold?
flashcards.back: Shards (replica sets): the data. Config server replica set: the chunk map and other metadata; the balancer runs on its primary. mongos: nothing; it caches the map and routes.

flashcards.front: When does the MongoDB balancer migrate a range?
flashcards.back: When the shards holding the most and the least of a collection differ by at least 3 chunk sizes (384 MB at the default 128 MB). One migration per shard at a time.

flashcards.front: What happens to inserts under a monotonically increasing shard key?
flashcards.back: They all go to the chunk whose range ends at MaxKey, on one shard, however balanced the stored data is.

flashcards.front: Which unique indexes can a sharded collection enforce across the cluster?
flashcards.back: Only ones on the shard key or starting with it. Even `_id` is unique only per shard when it isn't the shard key.

terms.plain: MongoDB's storage engine: B-tree files per collection and index, a cache, checkpoints every 60 seconds and a journal.
The time between the oldest and newest oplog entry: how long a member can be away and still catch up by replaying.
The number of an election. Each member votes at most once per term, so two candidates can't both win the same one.
The stateless router of a sharded cluster: it caches the chunk map and sends each operation to the shards that own the key.
The replica set holding the sharded cluster's metadata, including every chunk's range and shard; the balancer runs on its primary.
A contiguous range of shard key values owned by one shard; 128 MB by default.
A chunk over the chunk size that can't be split because all its documents share one shard key value.
A query without the shard key: mongos sends it to every shard and merges the answers (`SHARD_MERGE`).

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to shard the payments collection on `{ createdAt: 1 }` because "every report filters by date, and `sh.status()` will show the data balanced". Explain what happens to inserts, what the balancer does about it, and which key you'd use instead.
explain_back.answer: A ranged key keeps values in order, and each chunk owns a range. Every new payment has a later `createdAt` than all the others, so every insert lands in the last chunk, the one that ends at MaxKey, and that chunk lives on one shard. That shard's primary takes 100% of the writes. The balancer only looks at stored data: when shards differ by three chunk sizes it moves old ranges off the full shard, so `sh.status()` does look balanced, but the newest range never leaves, and the hot shard stays hot. In the Try-it, after eight migrations the next 1,000 entries all still went to shard1. Date filters on reports are a weak reason anyway, because reports can scatter or run on a reporting copy. For the payments core I'd use `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }`: the hash spreads the millions of accounts evenly, so inserts spread, and one account's payments stay together in time order, so the account screen, our busiest read, is a single-shard query. Idempotency claims go in their own collection keyed by the idempotency key, since a unique index must start with the shard key.

deeper.body:
The election details have one more dial. When a new primary is elected, it can spend up to `catchUpTimeoutMillis` copying newer writes that other reachable members have before it starts taking writes, which saves some `w: 1` writes from rollback at the cost of a slower failover. The protocol versions page promises that pv1 preserves confirmed `w: "majority"` writes; anything less is a matter of luck and timing, as lesson 8's rollback showed. Zhou and Mu's NSDI 2021 paper describes the protocol as derived from Raft, with one big difference: secondaries pull the oplog from a sync source (which can be another secondary) instead of the primary pushing to every follower. That's why a set spread over two data centres can have the far secondaries copy from each other and send one stream across the link.

MongoDB 8.0 added config shards: the config server replica set can also store application data, which saves a replica set in small clusters (`sh.isConfigShardEnabled()` tells you). 8.0 also added `moveCollection` and `unshardCollection` for unsharded collections, and since 7.0 `analyzeShardKey` scores a candidate key's cardinality, frequency and monotonicity from sampled queries. Run it before you shard.

Orphans matter for reads too. A shard still holding orphaned documents filters them out with a `SHARDING_FILTER` stage, which you saw at the top of each shard's plan in the Try-it's `explain()`. Reads at read concern `available` skip that filter and can return orphans, which is one more reason to leave read concern at its default for payments.

The AutoMerger joins adjacent chunks that sit on the same shard, so the chunk count doesn't grow forever as migrations cut ranges.
